title: The origin of Santa Claus
claim: Santa Claus is a real figure who delivers gifts to children everywhere on one night.
subject: Santa Claus
stage_note: trail mapped; sources not yet verified
plain_status: Taken literally — one figure, all children, one night — not supported. The figure's origin is real and datable; that trace is in progress.
summary: Origin trail: St. Nicholas of Myra → Sinterklaas → Moore (1823) → Nast → Coca-Cola. A worked example of tracing a claim to its source — mid-trace.
lede: A claim everyone grows up with, run through the same format as any other. Taken literally the claim fails — but the figure has a real, datable origin, and tracing that is the actual work. This entry is *mid-trace*: the trail is mapped, the primary sources aren't all confirmed yet.
author: Priority Nexus LLC

preamble.title: Under Investigation — this entry is a work in progress.

blocks.text: It's here to show what a claim looks like before the trace is finished: the trail is laid out, but each node stays marked "Unlocated" until the original source is pulled and read. Nothing here is called verified yet.

"Is Santa real?" is really two questions wearing one coat. One is literal — does a single person deliver gifts to every child in one night? That one is not supported. The other is historical — where does the figure come from? That one has a real answer, and it's the trail below. Keeping the two apart is the whole point of the format.
The documented path from a historical person to the modern image. No primary source has been pulled yet — the trail is built from general knowledge — so each node is marked **Unlocated**.

nodes.heading: ~300 — A real person — Nicholas of Myra
nodes.citation: Nicholas, 4th-century Christian bishop of Myra (in Lycia, in present-day Türkiye). Known through later accounts for anonymous gift-giving.

details.label: What it shows
details.text: There was a historical figure at the root of the tradition. The gift-giving stories around him come from later sources, not contemporary record.

details.label: Next step
details.text: Pull the earliest surviving accounts and date them, rather than relying on retellings.

nodes.heading: 1600s — Sinterklaas — the Dutch tradition
nodes.citation: The feast of St. Nicholas and the Dutch "Sinterklaas" gift custom, carried to North America by Dutch settlers.

details.label: What it shows
details.text: The name and the gift-bringer role that the English "Santa Claus" descends from.

details.label: Next step
details.text: Confirm the route from Sinterklaas to the American figure with dated primary sources.

nodes.heading: The poem that fixed the modern details
nodes.citation: "A Visit from St. Nicholas" ("’Twas the night before Christmas"), published anonymously in 1823, later attributed to Clement Clarke Moore.
nodes.quote: — the sleigh, the reindeer, the chimney, and the night before Christmas all appear here.

details.label: What it shows
details.text: Much of the specific modern image traces to one widely-read poem, not to ancient tradition.

details.label: Next step
details.text: Read the 1823 text at source and weigh the disputed authorship.

nodes.heading: 1860s — The look — Thomas Nast
nodes.citation: Thomas Nast's illustrations in *Harper's Weekly* (1860s–1880s), widely credited with the rotund, bearded, workshop-at-the-North-Pole image.

details.label: What it shows
details.text: The visual Santa was built up in the popular press over decades.

details.label: Next step
details.text: Locate the specific issues and dates.

nodes.heading: A sub-myth — "Coca-Cola made Santa red"
nodes.citation: Haddon Sundblom's Coca-Cola advertisements (from 1931) spread the red-and-white Santa widely.

details.label: What it shows
details.text: The ads popularized one version — but the claim that Coca-Cola **invented** the red suit is itself a drift: red-suited Santas appear well before 1931. A claim inside the claim, logged for its own trace.

details.label: Next step
details.text: Date pre-1931 red-suit depictions to settle the sub-myth directly.

sections.heading: What would settle it — next steps

items.text: **Finish the source trace.** Pull each node's primary source, read it, and move the node from "Unlocated" through to "Verified at source." That alone promotes this entry from Under Investigation to Traced.

**Separate the sub-claims.** The literal gift-deliverer, the historical origin, and the "Coca-Cola invented red Santa" myth are three different claims. Each gets its own verdict instead of one blurred answer.

blocks.text: Literal claim, as stated → not supported. Historical origin → real; trace in progress. "Coca-Cola invented red Santa" → likely a drift; test by dating earlier images.
